summary: Describes a forward error correction scheme for the RaptorQ code and its use in reliable delivery of data objects. RaptorQ is a fountain code with more flexibility, larger source block support, and better efficiency than the earlier Raptor codes in RFC 5053.

eli5.summary: Imagine sending a puzzle with extra spare pieces. Whoever collects enough pieces, any pieces, can rebuild the picture. RaptorQ is a clever way to do that for data, so lost packets do not need resending.

questions: how does raptorq forward error correction work
subtitle: A fountain code that lets a receiver rebuild a file from almost any sufficiently large set of packets, without asking for resends.

tldr.problem: When objects are delivered to many receivers or over lossy paths, retransmitting lost packets is costly. Senders instead want to add repair data that works no matter which packets are lost.
tldr.mechanism: RaptorQ splits an object into source blocks of equal-sized symbols, derives intermediate symbols from them, and generates as many repair symbols as needed from those. Each packet carries a 4-octet FEC Payload ID with a block number and symbol ID.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can usually recover a block from a number of symbols equal to the source symbol count, and the RFC requires failure rates of at most 1 in 100, 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 1,000,000 at K', K'+1 and K'+2 symbols.

today: RFC 6330 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC describes RaptorQ as the next generation of the Raptor code in RFC 5053.

sections.title: What RaptorQ Is For
sections.content:
This RFC specifies a Forward Error Correction (FEC) scheme for the RaptorQ code, used to deliver data objects. It follows the FEC scheme format defined in RFC 5052, and it is the next generation of the Raptor code in RFC 5053. The RFC says RaptorQ gives better reliability, better coding efficiency and support for larger source blocks than that earlier code.

RaptorQ is a fountain code: the encoder can generate as many encoding symbols as needed on the fly from the source symbols of a block. The decoder can recover the block from almost any set of encoding symbols of cardinality only slightly larger than the number of source symbols. It is also a systematic code, so the original source symbols are among the symbols that can be sent, along with repair symbols.

The scheme is a Fully-Specified FEC scheme with FEC Encoding ID 6. For background on FEC in reliable multicast, the RFC points to RFC 3453.
sections.eli5: Instead of resending the exact piece you lost, the sender keeps making fresh helper pieces. Any helper piece is as good as any other, so you just need to collect enough of them.

sections.title: Packet and Transmission Formats
sections.content:
All fields use network byte order. Every encoding packet carries a 4-octet FEC Payload ID: an 8-bit Source Block Number (SBN) naming the block the symbols belong to, and a 24-bit Encoding Symbol ID (ESI) naming the symbols in the packet.

The FEC Object Transmission Information (OTI) tells the receiver how the object was partitioned. The common part has the Transfer Length F (40 bits, at most 946270874880 octets) and the Symbol Size T (16 bits, in octets). The scheme-specific part has the number of source blocks Z (8 bits), the number of sub-blocks N (16 bits) and a symbol alignment parameter Al (8 bits). Together the encoded OTI is 12 octets.

The transfer length limit follows from the symbol size limit, the limit of 56403 symbols per source block, and the limit of 2^8 source blocks.
sections.eli5: Every packet has a small sticker saying which part of the file it helps with and which piece it is. A separate note says how big the file is and how it was cut up.

sections.title: Splitting an Object into Blocks
sections.content:
An object of F octets is divided into Z source blocks, numbered from zero, each coded independently. Each block holds K source symbols of T octets, and T MUST be a multiple of Al. The parameters MUST satisfy ceil(ceil(F/T)/Z) <= K'_max, where K'_max is 56403. The function Partition[I,J] splits a size into nearly equal parts. If the last symbol is short it is padded at the end with zero octets for encoding.

Each block can also be split into N sub-blocks small enough to decode in working memory. When N is greater than 1, a symbol is not a contiguous part of the object: the mth symbol is the concatenation of the mth sub-symbol of every sub-block. Section 4.3 gives an example algorithm for choosing T, Z and N from inputs such as the working-memory size WS and the maximum payload size P'. The recommended value of Al is 4, and one symbol per packet is RECOMMENDED, though receivers SHALL accept packets with several.

ESI values 0 to K-1 are source symbols and ESI values K onward are repair symbols. Each packet holds either only source symbols or only repair symbols, all from the same block, and each MUST contain whole symbols (except for padding in the last source symbol). The receiver does not need to know the total number of repair packets.
sections.eli5: A big file is cut into chunks, and each chunk into equal-sized pieces. Pieces numbered up to the chunk size are the real data; higher numbers are the helper pieces.

sections.title: The Encoder: Intermediate and Repair Symbols
sections.content:
To encode, the K source symbols are first padded with zero symbols up to K', the smallest value in the RFC's systematic index table that is at least K. Source symbols keep their ESIs, padding symbols get no ESI because they are never sent, and the encoder uses internal IDs (ISIs) so padding is treated like data.

The encoder then computes L intermediate symbols, where L = K' + S + H. These are uniquely defined by the source symbols and by pre-coding relationships: S LDPC (low density parity check) symbols and H HDPC (high density parity check) symbols. The intermediate symbols are also split into W LT symbols and P PI symbols, handled differently. The RFC gives an example method: build a matrix A so that A*C = D and solve for the intermediate symbols C, which can be done with the decoding process.

Each encoding symbol, source or repair, is then the sum of a few intermediate symbols chosen by a tuple (d, a, b, d1, a1, b1) from a tuple generator. That generator uses a pseudo-random function built on four 256-entry tables of 32-bit values (1024 numbers that sender and receiver must both have), a degree distribution table, and a per-size systematic index. The addition is the exclusive-or of octets, and multiplication uses the field GF(256).
sections.eli5: The sender first makes a hidden set of mixed-up helper pieces from the real ones. Then every packet is a small recipe adding a few of those hidden pieces together, and the same recipe book is known to both sides.

sections.title: The Decoder
sections.content:
Every received encoding symbol is a known combination of intermediate symbols, so together with the pre-coding relationships the receiver has a system of linear equations. Any method that solves it can decode; the choice only affects speed. Once the intermediate symbols are known, missing source symbols are regenerated with the encoding process.

The RFC describes an efficient example decoder that runs Gaussian elimination in a chosen order, using row and column reordering, and keeps the matrix sparse. It starts with the PI symbols "inactivated". The RFC states that the order of elimination does not change whether decoding succeeds, only how fast it is.

A compliant decoder SHOULD recover the whole block whenever it receives a mathematically sufficient set of symbols. With K' symbols whose ESIs are chosen independently and uniformly at random, it fails on average at most 1 time in 100. With K'+1 symbols, at most 1 in 10,000. With K'+2, at most 1 in 1,000,000. When N is greater than 1, a receiver can decode a whole block or one sub-block at a time depending on how much RAM it has.
sections.eli5: The receiver treats each packet as a clue in a big puzzle of sums and solves for the hidden pieces. With just a couple of extra clues, solving almost never fails.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Delivery can be attacked by sending corrupted packets that receivers accept as real. This matters most for multicast, where one corrupted packet injected near the root of the tree reaches many receivers. Even one corrupted encoding packet may produce a completely corrupted decoded object.

The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS source authentication and integrity checking of decoded objects before handing them to an application. Its example is appending a SHA-256 hash of the object before transmission and checking it after decoding, with a digital signature over the hash for source authentication. It also RECOMMENDS a packet authentication protocol such as TESLA (RFC 4082) to drop corrupted packets on arrival, and Reverse Path Forwarding checks in routers and switches to limit injection. Because some FEC information may come from a session description, forged descriptions should be prevented too.
sections.eli5: One fake puzzle piece can ruin the whole picture. So you should check that pieces and the finished picture really come from the sender.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: FEC Encoding IDs and FEC Instance IDs are subject to IANA registration, following the general guidelines in RFC 5052. IANA has assigned the value 6 under the ietf:rmt:fec:encoding registry to "RaptorQ Code" as the Fully-Specified FEC Encoding ID for this specification.
sections.eli5: The official list of codes now has a line saying that number 6 means RaptorQ.

fields.name: SBN
fields.desc: Source Block Number: which source block the symbols belong to.

fields.name: Encoding Symbol ID
fields.desc: Identifies the encoding symbols in the packet.

fields.name: Transfer Length (F)
fields.desc: Object length in octets, at most 946270874880.

fields.name: Symbol Size (T)
fields.desc: Size of a symbol in octets.
